title: First and Last Position of Target in Sorted Array
statement: You are given values, a list of integers sorted in non-decreasing order (duplicates allowed), and an integer target. Return a list of two integers [first_index, last_index], where first_index is the index of the earliest occurrence of target in values and last_index is the index of the latest occurrence. If target does not appear in values (including when values is empty), return [-1, -1]. Indices are 0-based. When target occurs exactly once, first_index and last_index are equal. A tempting mistake is to run one ordinary binary search, stop at any single matching index k, and return [k, k]: on inputs where target is duplicated, that binary search can land in the middle of the run and report a zero-width range instead of the true span. Locate both ends independently. Aim for O(log n) time using two boundary binary searches, one biased left to find the first occurrence and one biased right to find the last.
hints: A single binary search finds *an* occurrence of target, but which index does the problem actually ask for? If you return that one index for both ends, what happens when target is duplicated? Can you aim a binary search at the leftmost match specifically?

Run two binary searches. In the leftmost search, when values[mid] == target, record mid as a candidate and keep going left (right = mid - 1); in the rightmost search, record mid and keep going right (left = mid + 1). Never return mid immediately on a match.

Write find_edge(bias_left): loop while left <= right with mid = left + (right - left) // 2. On values[mid] == target set found = mid, then shrink toward the biased side; on values[mid] < target set left = mid + 1, else right = mid - 1. Return found (-1 if never set). The answer is [find_edge(True), find_edge(False)].
